en: Theragāthā 19.1 Paññāsanipāta First Chapter
The Verses of the Elder Tālapuṭa:
“When indeed shall I dwell alone,
without a companion, in mountain caves?”
Contemplating all existence as impermanent—
when will that state of mine come to pass? When indeed shall I,
a sage wearing tattered robes, become such?
Clad in saffron robes, free from possessiveness and desire,
having destroyed passion, hatred, and likewise delusion,
I shall dwell happily, having gone to the forest.
When, clearly seeing this body as impermanent— a nest of death and disease,
pursued by death and old age— shall I dwell free from fear?
Alone in the forest— when indeed will that time come?
When shall I [cut] the creeper of craving, which gives birth to fear,
brings forth suffering, and follows after manifold forms?
When, having taken up the sharp sword made of wisdom,
will I dwell having severed even that [craving]?
When indeed, with the fierce heat of the sword made of wisdom?
Having suddenly taken up the weapon of the seers,
when will that time come when I shall suddenly shatter Māra along with his host upon his lion-throne?
When indeed shall I be seen by the virtuous ones in their assemblies— by those who revere the Dhamma, the Tathāgatas,
who see things as they truly are, and have conquered their senses?
When indeed will that striving come to pass?
When indeed will weariness, hunger, thirst,
wind, heat, or insects and reptiles [not trouble me]?
They shall not afflict you in the Giribbaja;
when indeed will that state of one who has attained his goal come to pass?
When indeed will that which was known by the Great Seer [be realized]?
The Four Truths are very difficult to see;
when, being composed in mind and mindful,
shall I attain them through wisdom?
When indeed shall I, devoted to tranquility, perceive forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena as if they were ablaze?
When, through wisdom, shall I see this? When indeed,
having been addressed with harsh words,
shall I no longer be dejected because of that sign?
And even when praised for that sign, I shall not be elated; "When will this happen to me?
When indeed [will it be] with wood, grass, and creepers?"
When shall I weigh these aggregates and these immeasurable phenomena—
both those that are internal and those that are external— equally?
When indeed will the monsoon cloud,
with its fresh waters, drench my robe as I travel along the path frequented by seers in the forest?
When indeed will it rain? When,
in the forest, having heard the cry of the crested peacock,
the bird dwelling within the mountain caves?
Having risen up for the attainment of the Deathless, one should reflect:
"When indeed will that come to pass?
When indeed [shall I see] the Ganges, the Yamunā, and the Sarassatī?"
To Pātālakhitta and Vaḷavāmukha,
may I fly by means of psychic power without being obstructed—
when indeed will that terrifying time come?
When, like a snake moving unimpeded,
will you shatter your desire for the strands of sensual pleasure,
casting off all signs of beauty?
When will that time come when he is absorbed in jhāna? When,
like a poor man oppressed by debtors, having found a treasure,
will he satisfy his creditors?
"I shall be satisfied upon attaining the teaching of the Great Seer; when indeed will that happen?
For many years I have been petitioning you."
“Enough for you of this life at home”;
now that I have gone forth, for what reason,
O Citta, do you not apply yourself?
"Was I not indeed entreated by you, O Citta, [with the words]:
'In Giribbaja there are birds of variegated plumage,
thundering with a roar like the sound of Mahinda'?"
They will delight you as you meditate in the forest—
those friends and beloved kinsmen in the family,
the pleasures of play, and the strands of sensual desire in the world.
Having abandoned everything, you have come to this middle state;
yet even so, O mind, you are not satisfied with me.
This is mine alone; indeed, you do not belong to others.
What is the use of lamenting at the time of donning the armor?
Seeing that all this is unstable,
I went forth out of a desire to win the state of the Deathless.
The well-spoken speaker, supreme among bipeds,
the great physician, the charioteer who tames men:
"The mind is flickering, like a monkey," he said.
For one who has not yet abandoned passion, it is very difficult to restrain.
Indeed, sensual pleasures are variegated, sweet, and enchanting;
therein ordinary people, being ignorant, remain bound.
Seeking renewed existence, they desire suffering;
led by their own minds, they are cast down into hell.
[They dwell] in the forest resounding with the cries of peacocks and cranes.
"Surrounded by leopards and tigers, dwell under their control;
abandon all regard for the body and do not fail!"—
thus, O mind, did you formerly urge me.
“Cultivate the meditations and the faculties, the powers, the development of the factors of enlightenment and concentration,
and touch the threefold knowledge within the Buddha’s teaching.”
"Thus indeed, O mind, you formerly directed me:
'Cultivate the path leading to the attainment of the Deathless,
which is emancipating and conduces to the destruction of all suffering.'"
“The Eightfold Path, which purifies all defilements”—
thus indeed, O mind, you formerly urged me on.
“Regard the aggregates wisely as suffering.”
"Abandon that from which suffering arises;
make an end of suffering right here"—
thus, O mind, you used to urge me in the past.
"Contemplate wisely: 'It is impermanent, it is suffering';
see it as empty, selfless, a calamity, and a slaughter;
thus restrain the mental wanderings of the mind."
"Thus indeed, O mind, you formerly urged me on:
'Become shaven-headed and disfigured, come under a curse,
and wander among families for alms with a bowl in hand.'"
"Apply yourself to the words of the Teacher, the Great Seer"—
thus indeed did you formerly enjoin me, O mind.
"Walking well-restrained within the village streets..."
"With a mind unattached to lineages and sensual pleasures,
like the moon on the night of the full moon"—
thus indeed did you formerly enjoin my heart.
“Be a forest-dweller and an alms-food eater;
be a charnel-ground dweller and a wearer of rag-robes;
be one who never lies down, always delighting in the ascetic virtues.”
"Thus indeed you formerly urged me on, O mind;
like one who plants trees only to wish to cut down that very tree at its root once it has borne fruit."
You make this mind just like that,
when you yoke me to what is impermanent and fickle.
Formless, far-reaching, and wandering alone—
I will not carry out your word now;
for sensual pleasures are painful, bitter, and fraught with great fear—
I shall wander with my mind intent only upon Nibbāna.
It was not for lack of fortune, nor out of shamelessness,
nor for the sake of the mind, nor because of distance or longing;
it was not for the sake of livelihood that I went forth.
And I have given you this assurance in my mind:
"Fewness of wishes is praised by the true men,
as is the abandoning of reviling and the subsiding of suffering."
"Thus indeed, O mind, you directed me then;
now you go back to what was practiced before.
Craving and ignorance, and the pleasant and the unpleasant—"
Beautiful forms and pleasant feelings,
and the delightful strands of sensual pleasure— these have been vomited up;
I do not venture to drink them down again once they have been vomited.
In all respects, O mind, my word has been heeded by you;
through many births you have not been provoked to anger.
Your internal disposition arises from your gratitude.
For a long time you have wandered through suffering because of what was done by you.
You alone, O mind, make us a brahmin;
you make us a kshatriya, a king, and a ruler.
At times we were Vessas and Suddas,
and even by your very power we attained the state of gods;
it is solely because of you that we have become Asuras.
Because of you, we have become denizens of hell;
furthermore, at times we have even been among the animals or as hungry ghosts solely through your agency.
Surely you will deceive me again and again,
showing yourself like a puppeteer’s marionette;
you entice me like one who is mad.
Although you have been neglected by me,
formerly this mind wandered on its journey wherever it wished,
wherever it desired, and in whatever way it pleased.
Therefore, today I shall restrain it through wise means,
just as one who holds a goad restrains a rutting elephant.
And the Teacher has established this world for me.
As impermanent, unstable, and pithless—
leap forward, O mind, into the teaching of the Conqueror!
Deliver me from the great flood so difficult to cross.
This mind of yours is not as it was before;
I am no longer able to turn back under your control.
I have gone forth in the teaching of the Great Seer.
Those like me do not endure destruction.
The mountains, the oceans, the rivers, the earth,
the four cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, the nadir, and the zenith— these alone remain.
All three realms of existence are impermanent and afflicted;
where can you go, O mind, to find happiness?
What will you do with me, O mind, who am so frail?
One who follows the dictates of his own mind is not fit for this;
he would never touch a two-mouthed bellows—
fie on that full thing with its nine streams of flow!
Frequented by boars and deer,
with mountain slopes and crags naturally beautiful,
and with forests where the new rain has fallen during the monsoon;
There, having entered a cave-dwelling, you shall find delight.
There are birds with deep-blue necks, beautiful crests, and fine beaks,
whose wings and plumage are variegated.
Those who roar with a voice like that of Mañjughoṣa shall delight you as you meditate in the forest,
when the rain has fallen and the grass is four fingers deep.
In the forest in full bloom, resembling a mass of clouds,
I shall lie like a branch amidst the trees;
that ground will be as soft for me as cotton.
I shall indeed cultivate [the mind] as a master does;
even that which is obtained by others is sufficient for me.
I shall not cultivate it with such lack of diligence as they do.
Just as a cat’s pelt is well-beaten,
so shall I speak as a master;
whatever may be obtained by this, let that suffice for me.
By means of energy, I shall bring you under my control,
just as one skilled with the hook brings an elephant in rut under control.
For when you are well-tamed and steadfast, [I shall lead you to the highest state].
Like a horse trainer with a straight horse,
I am able to enter upon the auspicious path,
which is always frequented by those who guard their minds.
I shall bind it firmly to the object with strength,
as one binds an elephant to a pillar with a strong rope;
that [mind] of mine, well-guarded by mindfulness and well-developed, [shall remain].
You shall become independent of all states of existence.
Having cut off that which follows the wrong path with wisdom,
having restrained it with yoga, and having established it on the right path;
Having seen both the arising and the passing away, as well as the coming-to-be, you will become an heir to the Teacher of the Supreme Word.
You have been established under the sway of the four deceptions; [now, abandon them].
My mind has wandered like a village boy;
surely you will attend upon the Great Sage, the compassionate one who severs the bonds of the fetters?
Like a deer in a beautiful, well-wooded forest,
I shall delight in that untroubled mountain,
lovely with its clouds and garlands of rain.
Without doubt, O mind, you will go to the beyond.
Whatever happiness men and women experience who live according to your desire and under your control—
“O mind, your disciples are ignorant, following the sway of Māra, and delighting in existence.
… Thus spoke the Elder Tālapuṭa.
The Collection of Fifties is finished.
Therein is this summary verse: In the Collection of Fifties...
There was one palm-leaf manuscript, very pure;
therein were fifty verses,
and five more besides.
